title: The Promised Land: Text, Tradition, and Interpretation
desc: INSIGHTS & IDEAS: TUESDAY NIGHT LEARNING WITH GIDEON AMIR August 4, 11, 18, 25 | 7-8:30 PM ET Location: Zoom Classroom God promised Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob that their descendants would inherit the land of Canaan. After the Exodus from Egypt and forty years of wandering in the desert, the Israelites, under Joshua’s leadership, conquered the Promised Land and settled there. However, the biblical text raises difficult geographical and ethical questions. Join us to explore these questions and examine how they have been understood and addressed across generations.

title: Masada: The Untold Story
desc: In the year 74, Masada, a steep, diamond-shaped plateau overlooking the Dead Sea and Judean Desert, was the site of the last stand of Jewish rebels against Rome. They famously chose mass death rather than surrendering to the hated Romans according to the author of the single historical source. But what really happened? Historian Barry Strauss highlights how decades of research by archaeologists and historians, including exciting recent work, has helped unravel the mystery.

title: The Panama Canal: Power, Politics, and Ambition
desc: Historian Ralph Nurnberger argues why the Panama Canal can be seen as either a landmark achievement of American diplomacy or a symbol of U.S. arrogance and corruption. Closely tied to Theodore Roosevelt’s vision of global power, the canal became both a strategic success and a long-running controversy. Nurnberger traces its history, including the debate over transferring control to Panama, while examining why the United States built a canal in another country and why Panama was selected.

title: How to be a Jewish Adult
desc: Do you ever feel like you could use a handbook for how to build a Jewish life? If you identify as Jewish or Jew-ish but aren’t sure how to incorporate Judaism into your day-to-day life, this 8-week series led by guest Rabbi Loren Berman offers equal parts community-building and deep-dive into core lessons from our tradition to help you feel more Jewishly connected.

desc: The Grateful Dead has more than music to share: The band offers lessons on impermanence, interconnection, and the search for meaning, which author Casey Rae explores. Tracing the Grateful Dead’s connections to the Beat generation, psychedelia, and Eastern philosophy, Rae examines how the band’s music, community, and improvisational ethos reflect deeper questions about transcendence, identity, and human connection. title: The Mosaics of Ravenna: A Glittering Vision in Glass and Gold

These masterpieces, found in UNESCO-listed sites such as San Vitale and the Mausoleum of Galla Placidia, illuminate early Christian art. In this richly illustrated lecture, Columbia University art historian Sophia D’Addio explores their artistic innovations, symbolism, patrons, and enduring legacy. title: The Cuban Missile Crisis: Re-examining a Moment of Extreme Danger
desc: Most Americans know the basic story of the Cuban Missile Crisis: In 1962, the Soviet Union secretly placed nuclear missiles in Cuba, the United States discovered them, and after a tense 13-day standoff, the Soviets backed down. The episode is often cited as a model of effective crisis management. However, historian Allen Pietrobon revisits the crisis to argue that it was less a triumph of leadership than a near-disaster averted largely by luck and fear.

title: The Irrepressible Rosa Bonheur: “The 19th Century’s Most Famous Woman Artist”
desc: French artist Rosa Bonheur was one of the 19th century’s most celebrated animal painters. The first woman awarded France’s Legion of Honor, she gained international fame for her highly realistic works and dedication to studying animals firsthand—including at Buffalo Bill Cody’s Wild West Show. Known for her unconventional lifestyle (trousers, short hair, and smoking in public), Bonheur remains a compelling figure. In an illustrated lecture, art historian Nancy G. Heller examines her life, art, and lasting influence. (World Art History Certificate elective, 1/2 credit)

Using familiar songs by leading jazz artists, Sherwin introduces song form, the role of improvisation, and how musicians interact within a jazz ensemble to create the music listeners hear.

desc: Historian and author Alexander Mikaberidze explores the Dreyfus Affair, the case that profoundly shaped modern French political culture. Beginning with the wrongful conviction of Jewish army officer Alfred Dreyfus in 1894, he traces how the controversy exposed divisions over justice, authority, nationalism, religion, and citizenship. Mikaberidze highlights the role of antisemitism, Émile Zola and the rise of intellectual activism, and the political struggles that reshaped the French Republic, leaving a legacy for civil rights, press freedom, democratic accountability, and the rule of law.

title: “Keep Calm and Carry On": England's Home Front in World War II
desc: British government propaganda dubbed World War II “The People’s War.” Historian Julie Taddeo looks at the many ways in which civilians participated in the war effort, from the Home Guard volunteers of “Dad’s Army” to housewives who were reminded to “Make Do and Mend,” to child evacuees and those raising rabbits and collecting scrap metal. She also discusses how memories of World War II live on in British TV shows and films in the 21st century.

title: The Fairies of Winter: From Nisser to Huldufolk
desc: While most people think of fairies as small, sweet, human-shaped beings with butterfly wings who grant wishes, folklorists say that this tiny, sparkling version is a relatively new idea, and that, in fact, the fairies of older traditions are something much stranger. Among the most compelling are the fairies of winter. Folklorists Sara Cleto and Brittany Warman explore winter fairies from different cultures, including some who love porridge and one who will suck your breath away if she catches you alone on a mountain during a snowstorm.

title: Paul Simon's "Graceland": Days of Miracle and Wonder
desc: In 1984, Paul Simon’s new marriage was failing and his career was in danger of stalling. That summer, a bootleg cassette of township jive—the street music of South Africa—became his personal soundtrack. Simon grew determined to create a collaboration that included township jive musicians. The result was “Graceland,” which won two Grammys and sold 16 million records. Music historian Ashley Kahn unfolds the album’s history and impact, revealing Simon’s creative process, the controversies the music raised, and the forces that helped the album achieve mainstream popularity.

title: Palatine Chapel
desc: In the heart of Palermo, the Palatine Chapel represents a unique fusion of Norman, Byzantine, Islamic, and Latin artistic traditions. It was commissioned in the 12th century and reflects the multicultural character of Norman Sicily at its height. Italian Renaissance art expert Rocky Ruggiero highlights the chapel’s interior, where shimmering Byzantine mosaics depicting scenes from the Old and New Testaments cover the upper walls, set against richly carved wooden ceilings executed in the intricate muqarnas style of Islamic art. (World Art History Certificate elective, 1/2 credit)

title: Slavery and the American Revolution
desc: Historian Richard Bell of the University of Maryland explores the American Revolution through the experiences of enslaved and free African Americans. With more than half a million African Americans living in slavery at the war’s outset, the conflict created new opportunities to pursue freedom. British promises of emancipation drew thousands away from rebel enslavers, making the Revolution a struggle over slavery as well as independence. While most remained enslaved after the war, more than 6,000 escaped on British ships, including over 3,000 Black loyalists evacuated from New York in 1783.

title: Dickens Without the Humbug
desc: With gripping plots, memorable characters, and keen social insight, Charles Dickens became one of history’s most beloved storytellers. The author of David Copperfield , Great Expectations , A Tale of Two Cities , and A Christmas Carol enjoyed extraordinary fame during his lifetime. Author Daniel Stashower traces Dickens’ remarkable journey from childhood hardship to literary stardom, exploring both his triumphs and setbacks. Actor Scott Sedar brings Dickens’ enduring legacy to life with readings from some of his most celebrated works.

title: Mark Rothko’s Philosophy, Life, and Career
desc: Mark Rothko, a Russian-born American artist, felt like an outsider after immigrating to the U.S. at age 10. This sense of alienation shaped his Abstract Expressionist paintings, which he intended as spaces for viewers to confront deep human emotions and experience catharsis, much like Greek tragedies. Rothko grew frustrated that many people saw his richly colored works as decorative rather than engaging with their emotional and spiritual purpose. Join art historian Matthew Palczynski as he explores the life and work of this visionary artist. (World Art History Certificate elective, 1/2 credit)

title: Nazis in South America: Notorious War Criminals Who Escaped Justice
desc: Writer and lecturer Adam Tanner examines how many Nazi war criminals escaped justice after World War II. Disguised as refugees and aided by sympathetic clergy, thousands obtained false identities and fled to Latin America. Among them were Adolf Eichmann, Franz Stangl, and Josef Mengele, all linked to major Holocaust atrocities. While some evaded capture for decades, determined Nazi hunters eventually tracked down and prosecuted a number of them, though many escaped justice permanently.

title: Venice's Artistic Revolution
desc: Around 1500, Venice reached the height of its wealth and cultural influence, surpassing Florence. Its lagoon setting, unique light, and access to Eastern pigments inspired a revolution in painting. At its center was Giovanni Bellini, whose brushwork and mastery of oil color shaped Giorgione and Titian. In a richly illustrated program, art historian Nigel McGilchrist traces Venice’s artistic rise and its gradual decline as influence shifted northward to the emerging powerhouses of Antwerp and Amsterdam. (World Art History Certificate elective, 1/2 credit)

desc: In an era of rapid technological advancement and evolving cities, contemporary architecture has challenged traditional ideas about what buildings can be and how they shape lives. title: The Fourteenth Winton M. Blount Postal History Symposium - Revisiting American Postal History
desc: 2026 marks 250 years since the signing of the Declaration of Independence. To mark the occasion, the Fourteenth Blount Postal History Symposium will reexamine key developments and stories of over two hundred and fifty years of American postal history and consider lesser-known stories and new lines of inquiry. Sponsored by American Philatelic Society, American Philatelic Research Library, and the Smithsonian National Postal Museum

title: Holiday Charms in Fairmount Park - In Person
desc: In the late 18th century, Philadelphia was a thriving center of commerce and culture, and many of its wealthiest citizens built elegant country retreats along the banks of the Schuylkill River to escape the bustle of city life. Six mansions known as the “Charms” are among the few remaining from the dozens of villas that once lined what is now Fairmount Park. They offer a glimpse into the city's architectural, social, and cultural history. Experience the enchanting appeal of three “Charms,” transformed with period-inspired holiday decorations, on this tour.

title: Gunboat Philadelphia: Save the Revolution! Virtual Reality Experience

title: Tours | Arts of China
desc: Examine the diverse artistic and cultural traditions of one of the world’s oldest civilizations in this in-person, docent-led tour. Learn about Chinese artworks such as ritual bronze vessels, calligraphy, brush paintings in ink and color, and exquisite ceramics. Please meet at the West Building Information Desk for the tour. title: Rembrandt and the Dutch Golden Age
desc: Art historian Joseph Paul Cassar presents a chronological framework for studying Rembrandt's vast output, moving from his time as a young, ambitious prodigy in his hometown; his early success; the height of his societal and financial peak; years of hardship and more introspective work; and his poignant final years. Cassar discusses Rembrandt's works within the historical context of the time, outlining his legacy in painting, drawing, and etching. ( World Art History Certificate elective, 1/2 credit)

title: What Mantises Reveal About Insect Evolution
desc: Praying mantises are some of the most captivating predators in the insect world, with their raptorial forelegs, uncanny stillness, and swiveling heads that seem almost alert to a human observer. But mantises are just one branch of a larger family tree called Dictyoptera , which also includes termites and cockroaches, giving scientists a unique window into how such different lifestyles could have arisen from shared ancestry. Entomologist Jessica Ware explores the evolutionary history of mantises, examining their hunting behavior, physiology, and relationships to their Dictyoptera relatives.

title: Meditation and Mindfulness
desc: Register to join the sessions . Join a free online guided meditation. In these 30-minute sessions, DC-based meditation teachers lead a variety of mindfulness practices. Friday sessions take inspiration from art in our museum’s collections. All are welcome! No previous experience is required. title: Permanent Collection Tour
desc: The National Museum of Asian Art has over 46,000 artworks from across Asia. Enjoy some of the finest on a docent-led tour and learn about commonalities and differences in cultures, aesthetics, and ideas.

title: Tour | From the Louvre
desc: In From the Louvre: Masterpieces of Islamic Art , you can admire remarkable artworks created between the seventh and nineteenth centuries from a vast geographic area extending from Spain to India. This tour guides you through the exceptional selection of masterpieces, including a striking Syrian-Egyptian basin inlaid with silver figures, an enigmatic Andalusian bronze lion, and a monumental portrait of a Persian king covered with jewels. Meanwhile, learn about the extraordinary journeys these works took and how they were invested with power and new meaning along the way. Image: Signed by Muham

title: Conservation Cart Talk | Woven and Cast
desc: Centuries ago, Chinese artists created embroidery using tiny metal strips wrapped around silk. Hear from one of our scientists about the technology she used to identify these metals. In this talk, she reveals how the artists took advantage of minor details in the metal’s composition to create subtle shimmering effects. This research supports the exhibition Woven and Cast: Chinese Textiles and Japanese Metalwork from the Shirley Z. Johnson Collection .
